title: 5 ways to improve call connect rates in Germany
summary: Explore five ways to improve call connect rates in Germany, from number registration and call volume to local presence and pre-call outreach.
body_markdown:
If your outbound calls in Germany are reaching fewer people, review five areas: number registration, calls per number, local presence, number reputation, and outreach before the first call. This guide walks through each check and where to start this week.


We hear the same complaint from German teams, and it has a specific shape. A rep tests it themselves. They call thirty leads from the dialer, call the same thirty from their personal mobile the next day, and reach noticeably more people from the mobile. The conclusion writes itself: something is wrong with the dialer.


The reality is more useful than that, and more fixable. Your personal mobile isn't a better phone than your dialer. The difference is that it doesn't look like a dialer to the software sitting between you and the person you're calling.


That software is the whole story.


## Why are call connect rates falling in Germany?


The short version: Germany has no mandated caller-authentication standard, and that changes everything about how spam labeling works there.


In the US, there's a fix for this exact problem. Numbers get registered under STIR/SHAKEN and carrier verification programs, which let carriers confirm that a number belongs to a legitimate, registered business. It also gives you a route to correct a false spam label when one lands. It's not perfect, but it's a real lever.


Neither of those programs applies outside the US. For German numbers, that lever simply doesn't exist yet. If you've been buying new numbers, adjusting settings, and wondering why nothing you try inside your CRM seems to matter, this is why. The tools that normally fix this aren't available in this market.


Without that standard, spam labeling in Germany runs almost entirely on crowdsourced, app-based detection with apps like:


- Hiya, which now powers spam identification on Samsung devices and across O2/Telefónica
- RealNetworks-based filtering is used by Deutsche Telekom
- Clever Dialer, tellows, Should I Answer, and others


These systems flag numbers algorithmically, based on calling behavior. A number that is new, makes a high volume of short calls to many different people in a short window, and picks up a handful of "unknown" or "spam" taps from recipients gets labeled within days. It doesn't matter which provider issued the number or how legitimate your business is. The pattern is what gets flagged.


That has two consequences, and together they explain most of what German teams are seeing.


**Buying new numbers doesn't work.** A fresh number looks clean for a few days. Then you point the same high-volume dialing pattern at it, and it gets flagged again. That doesn't fix the problem. It just resets the timer.


**Your own phone reaches more people because it has no usage pattern attached.** You make a handful of calls a day, mostly to people you know, mostly longer than sixty seconds. No detection system has any reason to flag you. That's a real advantage, and it's also one you can't scale. The moment you dial like a sales team from that number, it starts looking like a sales team.


It's also worth saying that regulators aren't going to solve this for you anytime soon. The Bundesnetzagentur can fine and block egregious offenders, but it blocked roughly 1,400 numbers in all of 2023. Enforcement is reactive, and nowhere near the scale of the problem.


## 5 ways to improve call connect rates in Germany


### 1. Register your numbers with Hiya


This is probably the single most valuable thing you can do today, and most teams have never heard of it.


Hiya offers free number registration through Hiya Connect. It takes under a day, costs nothing, and gives you two things you don't otherwise have: visibility into each of your numbers' spam status, and a direct channel to correct false flags when they happen.


Given that Hiya now powers spam and verification on both Samsung devices and O2's network, one free registration covers a big chunk of the German mobile market.


Start here:[hiya.com/products/connect/number-registration](https://www.hiya.com/products/connect/number-registration)


### 2. Cut your per-number call velocity


The single biggest trigger for these detection systems is a burst of short calls to many different numbers in a short window. Which is, unfortunately, an exact description of what a power dialer produces.


You can keep the volume. You just have to spread it differently:


- Use a larger pool of numbers, with a conservative daily cap on each one.
- Warm up any newly purchased number gradually. Don't point a full campaign at a number on day one.
- Watch your short-call ratio. A number that produces mostly sub-20-second calls is building a bad reputation whether or not anyone taps "spam."


This is the change most teams resist, because it feels like slowing down. In practice, a smaller number of dials that actually connect beats a larger number that get silently filtered.


### 3. Double-check your local presence setup


Regulatory requirements for German numbers mean the number's area code has to match your registered business address. That's a compliance requirement, but it has a practical side effect worth checking.


Make sure the numbers you're dialing from actually match the geography of the leads you're calling. Calling Hamburg leads from a Munich-registered number undermines local presence even though the number is technically "local-looking." If your lead list spans regions and your number pool doesn't, you're losing connects for a reason that has nothing to do with spam labeling.


### 4. Check number reputation before answer rates collapse


Most teams discover a flagged number the way you'd discover a flat tire at 80kph: after the fact, from the results.


You don't have to. Free lookup tools let you check a number's reputation on demand.[tellows.de](http://tellows.de/) , Clever Dialer, and Hiya's own checker all work. Build a quick weekly habit of running your active numbers through one of them. You'll catch a flag in days instead of finding out three weeks later when a campaign underperforms.


### 5. Warm the channel before the first call


An SMS or email touch before the first dial means the lead recognizes the number instead of reflexively ignoring it (or worse, reporting it, which is the outcome that actually costs you).


This one lines up with a broader shift that has nothing to do with Germany. Cold, call-first outreach converts at roughly 1–2% per dial industry-wide now, down from 5–6% a decade ago. Leading with async channels and using the call as a later, higher-context touch tends to outperform a call-first cadence in most markets. Germany just punishes the old approach faster.


## How do German call connect rates compare?


We looked at our own data before writing this, because it's worth knowing whether German connect rates are genuinely broken or just following a trend.


Using calls longer than 60 seconds as a proxy for actually reaching a person, calls into Germany have moved from roughly an 18% answer rate three years ago to around 14% today. That's a real decline. It's also gradual and consistent, not a cliff, and it tracks with what's happening to phone answer rates generally, in every market.


The other thing we found: German answer rates are broadly in line with non-German answer rates in our data. Whatever is making calling harder in Germany is not, on the aggregate numbers, a Germany-specific collapse.


Two honest caveats on that. First, an aggregate can hide a bad experience for a specific team with a specific number pool and a specific dialing pattern. If your rate is 2%, "the average is 14%" is not an answer; it's a starting point for diagnosis. Second, comparing a VoIP number to a personal mobile line is not a like-for-like comparison. It never has been. A fairer test is your dialer against another VoIP provider serving the German market.


And the direction of travel matters more than the current number. Both iOS and Android now ship native AI call screening. The share of people who pick up an unrecognized number is going down everywhere, for everyone, regardless of which system places the call. Any strategy built on "more dials will fix it" is running into a wall that's still moving.


## How your CRM supports call follow-up


A connect rate is one number. What happens on and after the call is where deals are actually won or lost. Did the rep have context before they dialed? Did the follow-up happen without someone having to remember it?


That's the case for having your dialing live inside your CRM rather than beside it. When calls, transcripts, and lead context sit in one system, a rep opens a lead already knowing what's been said, and the follow-up is automatic. It's also, circularly, part of what improves connect quality: a call that opens with real context lands very differently than one that opens with "is now a good time?"


The teams doing best in hard calling markets generally aren't the ones with the most numbers. They treat the call as one touch in a sequence that already has momentum behind it.


## Your weekly call connect-rate checklist


If you're seeing this in your own numbers, do these three things first:


1. Register your active German numbers with Hiya Connect. It's free, and it's the fastest win available.
2. Run your current numbers through tellows or Clever Dialer and find out which ones are already flagged.
3. Look at your calls-per-number-per-day. If any single number is carrying a large share of your daily volume, spread it.


Then add an SMS or email touch ahead of the first dial on your next campaign and compare.


None of this is a single switch anyone can flip for you, and we'd rather say that plainly than promise a fix that doesn't exist in this market yet. What we can tell you is that these five things are the levers that exist today, and the teams using them are getting much better results than the teams buying new numbers and hoping.
